Approximate solutions to high-dimensional Schr\"odinger equations are crucial for fields ranging from material and chemical science to quantum biology. By applying high-probability bounds under various assumptions about data and model parameters, we establish conditions ensuring generalization performance. Our results validate that training data can be generated efficiently and that the network architectures require only modest sizes, even when training for extensive periods. We confirm these theoretical findings empirically across several test cases, including scenarios involving numerous dimensions.

Speech recognition and pitch detection are essential yet traditionally challenging areas due to the distinct nature of tones and background noise versus the onsets, plosives, and vibrato found in natural speech. While formant continuity serves as a reliable indicator for tonal sounds, frictionous or explosive onsets can obscure these traces; consequently, a robust categorization strategy is crucial for effective system design. This paper introduces a novel method to classify speech sounds and follow tonal features, relying primarily on the statistical variations of energy and zero-crossing rates processed through a forward-backward Kalman filter. Energy values and zero-crossing rates are treated as observations of an underlying, unmeasurable state representing the signal's category (tone or speech). Employing a piecewise constant Markov model, this approach alternates between tones and speech based on the probabilial evolution of that latent state, alongside a simplistic pitch estimation derived from the duration of tonal segments. Experimental validation using the enhanced 1600-word TIMIT database confirms that the proposed system successfully tracks and detects pitch and reliably distinguishes between speech and tones, even in the presence of background noise.

Although deep neural architectures have recently yielded numerous state-of-the-art results in computer vision and deep learning, current architectural designs are often constrained by specific structural constraints, leading to limited performance and interpretability. This study introduces a method utilizing Property Directed Synthesis (PDS)—an automated programming technique—to architect high-capability and explainable neural networks. By framing the creation of network structures as a search problem, PDS-driven design search is used to automatically generate a set of new architectures. Experiments confirm that this approach not only identifies two new, state-of-the-art models for convolutional computer vision tasks but also validates that the resulting architectures are both human-understandable and easy to modify.

Beamforming is essential for managing data transmission in millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems, and pre-selected beam pairs are typically used to establish links. However, these links often experience blockages due to the dynamic movement of users and environmental changes. In a multi-group scenario, obstructed connections can cause inter-group interference, reducing overall spectral efficiency. This paper introduces a hybrid encoding (HE) multi-group broadcasting framework that enhances robustness by providing diverse alternatives for a given information set. By leveraging mmWave characteristics, the proposed framework identifies the optimal pre-established beam pair for each group to minimize missed detections. Consequently, using HE allows each group to select a suitable transmitter based on current conditions, enhancing link reliability and mitigating issues linked to Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed framework achieves greater resilience against link failures and lower blocking rates compared to conventional multibeam systems, while also delivering improved performance in terms of interference management and increased data transmission rates when utilizing standard parameters.

Federated Learning (FL) serves as a leading framework for private machine learning, yet communication bottlenecks often hinder practical FL deployments. Federated Distillation (FEDiS), an end-to-end learning technique, has emerged as a remedy for low FL model quality. However, current Distillation mechanisms fail to consider communication efficiency. In this work, we introduce a new framework termed Communication-Efficient Federated Distillation (CEFDiS). Unlike standard distillation where a single round consumes one communication cycle, our communication-inefficient approach requires multiple rounds within a single transmission. To address the risk of overfitting, which could arise from multiple updates in one message, we incorporate regularization. Furthermore, we optimize communication costs by employing adaptive protocols, transforming the problem into a communication-minimization task that can be solved using a linear programming approach. Comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that CEFDiS delivers superior performance and enhanced communication efficiency. Additionally, the proposed approach exhibits robust resilience against malicious attacks.

Software development demands prolonged efforts and involves the coordinated efforts of numerous team members, so developers depend on development management tools, such as issue tracking systems, to effectively handle the evolution of design concepts, code implementations, bug fixes, performance enhancements, and performance management. However, software projects often suffer from the "communication bottleneck," where the efficient handling of software issues is hampered by the inability to communicate effectively. To overcome this hurdle, we have assembled a unique, large-scale dataset compiled from 592 public Jira repositories. Our analysis reveals that these repositories represent a broad spectrum of software development activities. Furthermore, we have prepared the data for open-source release to facilitate developers in assessing the applicability of this data for their research, and to gain insights into development practices within the software industry, and to understand the characteristics of software development in the wild.

In distributed machine learning, the core objective is to minimize a total convex objective function across $n$ participants, each possessing their own local dataset. The objective function comprises a weighted sum of $n$ component functions, with each agent holding one unique function and their total weights and counts remaining unknown. To address this, we introduce a methodology grounded in a specifically designed nonlinear class of aggregation functions. Assuming each agent performs $\mathcal{O}(1)$ operations per iteration, the computational complexity for the proposed algorithm is $\mathcal{O}(n\log^2{n} + n\tau)$, where $\tau$ signifies the iterations required to reach $\varepsilon$-optimality $\tau \propto \log^2{\frac{L}{\varepsilon}}{\cdot}\left(1 + {1\over w_{\min}}\right){2}$; here, $\L$ represents the Lipschitz constant, and $w_{\min}$ denotes the smallest weight among the $w_i$ values. Each agent is required to execute $\tau$ iterations of one-dimensional binary searches, with every single iteration of the process necessitating communication across the entire agent network. Our approach simplifies complexity compared to existing methodologies by streamlining operations, and we provide a rigorous mathematical justification for this innovation, supported by empirical demonstrations that verify the method's practical utility in a 2D-parallelized setting where agents communicate only with immediate neighbors.

This study introduces an innovative multi-diffraction optical architecture designed to facilitate atom-cavity interaction across three distinct functional stations: (i) trapping and reading out, (ii) guiding and stabilizing, (iii) transporting and aligning, aimed at streamlining the fabrication of solid-state quantum memory devices. We demonstrate that light can be precisely directed to three targeted areas by engineering a quantum interference pattern within a microfabriculated on-chip non-reflective optical taper, achieving a non-uniform field distribution characterized by a central main lobe flanked by two side lobes. Specifically, the precisely sized main cavity is occupied by a high-taper reflective area, while the side lobes are positioned over low-taper reflective zones to execute our proposed quantum memory configuration. By occupying the main lobe with a quantum memory readout station, while the side lobes are used for trapping/staging, the system allows for efficient manipulation of trapped atoms into the main or side lobes, respectively, thereby enhancing the practicality and performance of future quantum memory systems.

Let $\Lambda^*$ be the free monoid formed from an alphabet $\Lambda$. This paper demonstrates that the MacNeille completion of this monoid, denoted $m(\Lambda^*)$, is equivalent to $s(\Lambda)$, which consists of all countably infinite sequences from $\Lambda$ subject to finite identification ($m/\Lambda^*`). Furthermore, elements of $m(\Lambda)$ are defined as closed subsets of the countably infinite powers of $\Lambda$, $\Lambda^\mathbb{N}$. These structures are organized into a complete idempotent right alternative ring featuring multiplication as a right-dominant operation. Finally, we illustrate that elements of $s(\Lambda)$ can be interpreted as infinite words exhibiting specific closure properties under closure complementation and infinite concatenation.

The rapid development of molecular engineering and synthetic biology relies heavily on comprehensive chemical databases. This study introduces an algorithm that generates polymer sequences capable of approximating target molecules—such as pharmaceuticals, agricultural chemicals, and petrochemicals—within a specified error margin. By representing each molecule as a mathematical vector containing numerical counts for specific chemical substructures (moieties), the problem is formulated to find an integer linear combination of moietic vectors that closely matches the target vector. This formulation was resolved using various polymers as vectors and the target vectors constructed from target molecules to obtain accurate solutions via solvers like CPLEX. While multiple valid solutions typically arise, the protocol includes a post-processing utility to select a single, representative polymer from these options.

We examine multiple aspects, such as selecting appropriate datasets, trancription algorithms, and techniques to improve output through active learning and model fine-tuning using corrected transcripts. Additionally, we address the generation of appropriate visual representations, or embeddings, to effectively organize and display these captioning results.

When data dimensions are small relative to the number of features, classical high-dimensional regression methods struggle. We address this regime by introducing a high-dimensional empirical characteristic function-based classifier that performs well even when features outnumber sample sizes. By utilizing charactericit functions to estimate conditional first- and second-moments, our approach automatically handles heteroscedasticity while remaining model-agnostic. Under mild assumptions, theoretical performance bounds demonstrate that the error of the complementary cumulative distribution function decreases exponentially with the sample and feature counts, while empirical risk analysis reveals optimal risk scaling with respect to both the number of features, total dimensionality, and underlying sparsity. These theoretical insights suggest that the empirical risk minimization framework provides substantial benefits: nearly optimal regression predictions via unknown error modeling and near-optimal classification success rates. Beyond theory, experiments reveal that a simplified version delivers nearly perfect regression accuracy and classification rates in scenarios as challenging as $1,000$ features against $10$ samples.

For an infinite, simple, connected, and locally finite graph $G$, the spectral dimension, denoted as $d_{s}(G)$, represents the limit: 
$$d_{s}(G)=2\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\log n}{\log i_{n}(G)}$$where $i_{n}(G)$ signifies the number of vertices within graph distance $n$ from a specific starting point. Conversely, the Ahlfors regular conjugal aidless (ARCM) measure exponent, denoted as $d_{m}(G)$, is defined as 
$$d_{m}(G)=2\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\log n}{\log I_{n}(G)}$$where $I_{n}(G)$ represents the number of edges connected to at most $n$ segments of path originating from a fixed vertex. This work establishes a relationship between these concepts and proves that if such a graph $G$ is not just any structure but one that possesses a regularity where the above regularity condition is satisfied (which implies in particular that the ratio of the log growth rates is well-behaved), then it guarantees that the spectral dimension cannot exceed the measure exponent, specifically showing that $d_{s}(G) \leq d_{m}(G)$.

Blending offers a simple method for selecting a physical solution to avoid unphysical outcomes such as density becoming negative or exceeding the local sound speed. Whether using the enthalpy as a prognostic variable, the approach of M\"ullers and others, or using pressure, Bluestein's method, or any other variant, all these techniques can be understood as specific geometric paths connecting the two mathematical solutions for density. We demonstrate that a path defined by minimally maximizing enthalpy—which we argue is both robustly physical and theoretically sound—is preferable for stability. To achieve this physical density calculation, we implement a blending strategy with the invariant fields of the $SU(2)_L$ flavor symmetry, specifically mixing $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesonic states.

This research introduces three distinct methodologies for constructing signature templates from data and evaluates their efficacy through extensive testing. The study further examines the internal consistency, complexity, and reproducibility of online signature templates by leveraging large datasets. Findings from this work are anticipated to provide significant implications for developing robust systems capable of validating digital transactions and authenticating user identities.

We identify the CFT data characterizing perturbative supergravity theories based on symmetric orbifolds of asymmetric $6|6$-dimensional complex orbifolds with Hamiltonian $H=1$. This data comprises primary fields that are symmetric under the orbifold $\mathbb{Z}_n$ action and scalar fields possessing conformal dimension $\Delta = 2 + j$, corresponding to spin $j$ of arbitrary arbitrary magnitude, as well as leading terms for the 4-loop and higher non-perturbative contributions to their 2-point correlations. By leveraging this information, we demonstrate the validity of the "bootstrap" inequality regarding the maximum two-loop coupling constraints in $N=6$ superconformal theories and establish the existence of universal, derivative-based bounds on higher-loop coupling dependencies. These results are reinforced by explicit computations of the model's 2-point and some 4-loop correlation functions.

Topological defects in 2D superconductors often induce higher-order spectral features called spin-vortex states (also known as magnetic-polarvortex or magnetivortex states). These quantum states are defined by their topological charge $|Q|=1$ in 2D superconductors. Our work reveals an interesting addition: in the environment around a localized charge-defect, these spin-vortex states are accompanied by higher-order spectral features with topological charge $|Q|=2$. We have numerically investigated this addition both in the case of a point-charge-defect as well as in more general geometries. Our results indicate that the local electric-field strength around the defect-modification controls the position and the energy-level separation, which can be quantitatively explained by a model that simulates a classical-like (non-quantum) particle in a modified effective potential: one that combines the Landau-Peierls gauge potential with the attraction/repulsion due to the fixed defect-charge. This effectively models how the defect-charge pulls or pushes the defect-charge into position, thus modifying the location and spacing between spin-vortex states.

While carbon and oxygen are heavily favored in big-bang nucleosynthesis due to the exceptional stability of the ${}^{4}\text{He}$ nucleus and the triple-alpha process creating the nearby-mass, tightly bound ${}^{12}\text{C}$, nitrogen synthesis is significantly hindered. This occurs because reactions proceeding through the ${}^{14}\text{N}$ bottleneck are severely impeded by the slowness of the intermediate ${}^{14}\text{O}$ capture. Previous estimates suggested this difficulty was nearly fatal to nitrogen production; however, this study demonstrates that the standard Big-Bang model can actually generate significant nitrogen levels if the initial temperature exceeds approximately $1.5 \times 10^9$ Kelvin. Given that primordial conditions are believed to have easily met this thermal threshold, these findings suggest that certain organic molecular structures could potentially be primordial.

This introduction gives a brief overview of the background of SML and explores the challenges associated with working in SML or developing tools and applications for SML or that serve the SML community. We hope that this work will encourage the researchers in SML or research institutions to build repositories of resources and focus on developing tools for SML or that serve the SML community. This paper is based on a presentation that the authors made at the first meetup at the at the at the at the ATML 2021.

In the rapidly evolving field of biomedically inspired graph modeling, this study presents a comprehensive survey. We begin by outlining key challenges in biomedicine and examining various graph representations used to encode medical knowledge, which serves to inspire novel graph learning approaches. Consequently, we survey state-of-the-art methodologies, categorizing nodes and edges within biomedicine, visualizing these complex graphs, and leveraging them for specific tasks such as recommendation, graphical encoding, and inference. Finally, we address current limitations and propose directions for future research in this area.

We enhance constraints on left-right symmetric models and inelastic dark matter scenarios involving momentum-dependent nucleon scattering, specifically within the momentum halo of White Dwarfs, by 10 to 100 times using recent astrophysical observation. This analysis also addresses critical uncertainties, including the density and temperature profile of White Dwarfs, their chemical age and cooling mechanisms, and the intrinsic luminosity caused by dark matter accumulation in their cores.

Graph databases are increasingly prevalent, and as such, graphs containing sensitive information are increasingly common. We introduce the Graph Privacy Calculator, a tool that determines whether a given graph database adheres to semantic-level privacy standards. Sematic privacy ensures that no sensitive data can be inferred from what is known, and evaluating it traditionally requires checking every possible semantic instance, an effort that quickly becomes computationally prohibitive. We address this bottleneck by constructing a specialized content-driven dependency graph tailored to the structural and attribute specifics of a given dataset. This approach allows privacy compliance to be assessed by examining a manageable set of critical paths within the graph, significantly reducing the computational load. Our methodology is highly efficient, with both the model construction validity checks operating in linear time, making it suitable for large-scale implementations.

The CP2K software package efficiently performs ab initio molecular dynamics using either real-space integration or plane waves for electronic spaces. It supports hybrid or semi-local treatments for exchange-correlation functions and can utilize either semi-empirical methods or pseudo-potentials for electronic structures. The implementation covers plane-wave basis sets with either real-space or grid-based integration, as well as real-space grids. The code is highly parallelized and optimized for mass-parallel computing infrastructures, including systems with trillions of transistors. This paper details the technical challenges and strategies involved in scaling CP2K toward exascale computing.

Hard X-rays emitted from the solar corona primarily result from solar flares, which significantly alter solar atmospheric conditions. These energetic particles gain energy through collisions, climbing up the atmospheric temperature scales and producing a "two-body" hard X-ray spectrum characterized by an exponential decay. However, at very low intensities, statistical variations dominate, causing deviations from this classic two-body model. This study identifies these statistical effects as the source of X-ray emission from a quiet sun region observed by the Solar Dynamics Observatory's Atmospheric Imaging Analyzer (ATLAS), a form of transient emission that had previously been missed. Using data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory's Atmospheric Imaging Analyzer (ATLAS), we observe structures within the two-body spectrum that correspond closely with loops in the loops that make up the SDO/ATLAS corona. These are likely formed in a similar way, but in a more quiescent way, as opposed to the more active nature of the solar flares.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective for various graph-structured prediction tasks. However, their typical setup, which relies on node-level labels and data splits, often results in significant performance drops when node attributes are sparse or unavailable during labeling. Existing methods for addressing sparse data, such as using node classes or employing transductive learning by labeling an entire test set at once, often lack real-world practicality. To bridge this gap, this study introduces "Train and Test Duration Augmentation" (TrainTest-time Duplication), a novel technique that simulates the slower accumulation of real-world labels. By training and testing in a cumulative manner, this approach significantly enhances model performance in sparsely labeled scenarios. The method was evaluated across six real-world datasets to compare train/test dynamics under both instantaneous and gradual data accumulation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by 10% to 50%. Furthermore, the authors developed an open-source package that implements this augmentation strategy for easy integration into GNN workflows.

This article explores how conformal field theory central charges are determined by the underlying conformal field's geometry through an analysis of the corresponding Euler-Arnold equation. We demonstrate that any such central charge must satisfy specific algebraic constraints derived as direct consequences of these conformally available constraints. Specifically, an exception free exceptional algebra $\mathfrak{v}$ is shown to necessate a central value of $1/11$ for its associated theory. Moreover, exceptional isotopies are employed alongside representation theoretic methods to derive several significant implications from these geometric requirements.

This study addresses the problem of determining the best system of $n-1$ mutual intersections of lines in $\mathbb{R}^n$ to estimate an unknown point $p$. Each connecting line is defined by $n$ measurements subject to Gaussian noise, representing a modern, noisy observation of the classic distance triangulation problem. We examine a maximum-likelihood framework and demonstrate its equivalence to a newly proposed method termed Complete Least Squares (CLS). SL solves a single linear system requiring no iterative processes. When measurement noise is minimal, the primary focus becomes minimizing the condition number of the CLS matrix; we analyze how this condition number responds to inputs and present an efficient reordering strategy. This approach ensures optimal performance by $p$ regardless of the initial observation configuration.

Standard thermal universe evolution models following inflation typically assume that every particle species contributing to the total energy density fully thermalizes within our visible sector. Conversely, our universe may instead harbor invisible sectors governed by their own Frank-Hubble mechanisms, resulting in particles that drive cosmic expansion but remain inaccessible to direct detection. If these hidden sectors exist, they could alter both the quantity and identity of the thermal degrees of value driving the post-inflationary universe, a factor critical to accurately computing the present-day relic abundance of dark matter. In this context, we investigate the consequences of nonthermal cosmological evolution within such hidden frameworks and explore whether multiple reheating phases emerge. Specifically, we analyze the stability of dark matter relics under these new conditions.

This work describes a search for same-sign W boson pair production during proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV using the LHC's CMS experiment. Data were collected with an integrated luminosity of $35.9 \, \text{fb}^{-1}$ from runs in 2016, 2017, and 2018. The search targeted events containing two same-sign leptons (electrons or muons) and two jets in a control region enriched with resonant W bosons, where the observed background levels aligned well with standard model predictions. After evaluating signal regions, the results showed no significant excess beyond the standard model, leading to constraints on various beyond-the-standard model parameters, specifically the electroweak production of same-sign W pairs via charge or flavor non-unitarity in the lepton sector, as indicated by a $\chi^2$ analysis.

**We introduce a new problem area known as cross-camera deep tinting, enabling the synthesis of simulated images matching the characteristics of various target cameras when working with footage from source sensors. High demand for this technique exists due to its utility in standardizing diverse camera inputs, particularly for medical and security surveillance where footage must be normalized for effective comparison. To achieve this, we propose a generative approach utilizing a conditional generator built around a ResNet-ECANet encoder paired with an Autoencoder-style component. Furthermore, we curated the largest publicly available tuning dataset, consisting of 1,000 matched image pairs across 10 distinct cameras. In a comprehensive evaluation involving eight existing methods and four specialized synthesizers, our model significantly surpassed current benchmarks. The accompanying software can be found on our provided research GitHub repository.**

We present findings from the most extensive dataset to date on cosmic shear, which consists of 138 comparisons of galaxy catalogues. The composition likely includes three major surveys—SDSS, NVSS, and WAPS—repeated multiple times against various backgrounds. Our results indicate cosmic shear is consistent with the standard $\Lambda$CDM model's predictions regarding matter and luminosity density, but observed lensing effects are more pronounced at redshifts $z>1$ than the model allows, suggesting potential issues with data systematics or a lower level of clustering than currently assumed. While the dataset lacks the volume to definitively test the assumption of a flat geometry, it strongly suggests curvature is negative at a confidence level exceeding 99%. Furthermore, the data confirm that spatial curvature exhibits a redzone dependence, detecting a clumpiness signature that rises sharply from near zero at $z=1$ to approximately 99% at $z=10$. At this high-redshift limit, the measurement corresponds to an excess of matter clustering beyond what the $\Lambda$CDM framework permits.

Software maintenance involves long-term, repetitive efforts to refine existing system functionality. This study explores a form of distributed or meta-maintenance, targeting a novel dimension by examining a real-world context where multiple developers work on identical files within the same project. By analyzing 17 major software projects on GitHub—collecting 478.1 million lines of code across 112,000 commits by 211,000 contributors across nine years—researchers discovered that concurrent editing of the same files is extremely common, occurring in 11% to 74% of line commits. Furthermore, 43% to 51% of these identical modifications are functionally equivalent, such as the same change applied to consecutive lines. These patterns suggest that a meta-approach to maintenance is viable, as there is significant duplication in work where multiple contributors make identical adjustments to the same code.

This study presents photometric and spectroscopic data for the $\gamma$ Doradus candidate BD And. Our analysis reveals it to be a detached eclipsing binary system with an orbital period of 0.51296 days, comprising a $0.337\,M_\odot$ primary and a $0.272\,M_\odot$ secondary star, with masses constrained via high-precision spectroscopy. Additionally, we identified two distinct $12.5$-minute pulsation modes: one is spatially regular but not periodic in amplitude and phase variation, and the other is periodic on a long-term timescale. By the end, the system is classified as a confirmed $\gamma$ Doradus binary.

User collaboration is critical to the success of recommendation algorithms. Existing collaborative approaches seek a user's global preference by aggregating information across multiple users using their item ratings as the primary data source. Nevertheless, these methods often neglect other relevant user-item contextual data. In response, we introduce *MD-CPR*, a novel multi-domain collaborative modeling framework designed to exploit comprehensive contextual attributes. Our approach divides items into several sparse domains based on the relevance of specific user features within each context. We map each domain into an independent latent space to capture domain-unique item characteristics, while simultaneously modeling the shared preferences that underpin all domains through item features. Furthermore, we establish a multi-level attentive drug interaction mechanism to weigh the significance of domain information and user preferences at both individual and global levels. Empirical evaluations on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks.

The least squares estimator remains a cornerstone solution for regression analysis due to its simplicity and robust performance. Yet, its effectiveness can diminish significantly in the presence of noisy samples. This study introduces a confidence interval for the optimal least squares estimator, specifically tailored to account for noise contamination. A central component of the proposed methodology is a novel concentration inequality applicable to functions of Gaussians that satisfy Pearson's condition of $\chi$-boundedness. Functioning as a streamlined version of the broader sub-Gaussian constraint, this new inequality maintains sharpness against minimally noisy datasets while offering an optimized constant for cases involving heavily noisy data. Empirical simulations validate the confidence intervals proposed in this work, demonstrating their superior reliability when data contamination is present.

This study introduces a framework for soliton interactions in three-dimensional scalar field theories lacking rotational $SO(2)$ symmetry at the third quantitative level ($\mathcal{O}(3)$ in nonlinearity). We devise a third-order equation of motion incorporating up to $R^2$ terms, where $R$ denotes the solitonic charge vector. The construction relies on solving a specific boundary-value problem. A key distinction of this approach from standard theories with invariance is the absence of a U(1) symmetry, a feature that significantly reduces both the difficulty and solution space. Notably, our theory accommodates single solitons of three distinct types: breathers, which oscillate temporally; and static bright solitons or anti-solitons, stable states or decaying modes respectively, each defined by a specific set of charges. These theories also exhibit non-trivial two-soliton scattering behaviors, including switch-on/switch-off dynamics and position-dependent sign changes.

Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) involves inferring the underlying reward function of an agent by observing its behavior. A common assumption in traditional IRL is access to a fully controllable environment; however, in many real-world scenarios, external forces can influence the system, causing the actual state trajectory to diverge from what would occur under the action model alone. Consequently, these external factors must be explicitly accounted for. In response, we introduce a hierarchical Bayesian approach designed to handle partiallly-regulated environments by introducing a latent variable to capture the cumulative effect of external influences on the state trajectory. Experimental results across various Maze navigation and Partial Navigation Networks confirm that our proposed framework effectively recovers reward functions in both navigation contexts.

This paper addresses the problem of determining when small loop transfer within minimal modular neighborhoods of loops is obstructed by modular neighborhood preservation in the group of homeomorphisms of the circle, by utilizing the loops' non-abundancy relative to various types of free groups. To achieve this analysis, the concepts of small loop transfer areas with respect to the fundamental group of the surface and these specific subgroup patterns are introduced. The study also explores how this non-abundance interacts with the properties of the loops being examined. As a concluding application of the theory, the presentation of the fundamental group of the knotted torus, referred to as the Clark torus, is achieved.

Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) serves as an effective methodology for determining optimal policies across various sequential decision-making scenarios. While RL offers a valuable tool for addressing dynamic control problems, its successful deployment necessitates careful consideration of distinct operational challenges. This paper investigates specific difficulties inherent to RL control and demonstrates their mitigation through a two-phased approach. Initially, a simplified model acquires the optimal policy via Deep RL, which subsequently transfers the acquired knowledge to the real-world environment by acting as a expert guide or generator of prioritized training data for the control agent. Utilizing this strategy in conjunction with Deep RL, we address two distinct and demanding control tasks: the regulation of cart-pole systems within stochastic contexts and the navigation of a mobile robot within complex indoor settings.

This study investigates whether a subpopulation of direct black hole (BH) seeds forms with substantial masses ($M \gtrsim 10^2$ M$_\odot$) in early Universe conditions. Such an existence could potentially explain the emergence of the most massive BHs. We utilize the initial conditions of the cosmological $\Lambda$CDM model to conduct Direct N-body simulations, tracking growth through dynamical and accretive mechanisms. The analysis covers the formation of BHs within the range of $10^4$-$10^8$ M$_\odot$ across redshifts $z$ = 6 to 1. By examining the initial mass function (IMF) of these direct BHs and their subsequent accretion, we find that while a "peaked" IMF is favored, a "flat" distribution is also viable. Inelastic neutron scattering provides access to both the dynamic and static structural aspects of materials by yielding data that, ideally, reflect the product of a joint area in momentum and real space, alongside some convolution with experimental resolution. However, interpreting this data is complicated because it requires the reduction of raw intensity to specific components, such as single-phonon contributions or magnetic excitations, to enable physical understanding. This paper introduces a method for analyzing inelastic neutron scattering via calibrated and interpretable neural networks. A U-Net convolutional architecture is trained against labeled spectral labels to automatically identify and label data; once trained, inference can be performed on new, previously unseen datasets. This approach is demonstrated using synthetic inelastic neutron scattering data generated from a two-oscillator model, where each component carries a distinct intensity.

Over the past few decades, open access preprint services have become essential components of research communities across various disciplines serving as primary venues for sharing work, and they will likely continue to do so. This study explores the current landscape of preprint services by reviewing their historical Lister, examining researcher attitudes through a global survey, and analyzing typecasting phenomena across different scientific fields by examining publication patterns over time. Evidence suggests that researcher adoption will likely increase in the near term, and preprints will probably supersede traditional publication channels as the dominant method for initial research dissemination.

Since physics education research (PER) is underrepresented in physics education literature because laptops often clutter lab tables, we suggest this allowance may help resolve such logistical challenges.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a cutting-edge material category defined by the near-equal distribution of at least five different metallic elements. Their intricate multi-component nature renders them difficult to investigate using conventional material science approaches, but this very complexity drives their exceptional properties. Consequently, significant effort has been devoted to integrating machine intelligence (MI) and machine learning (ML) into alloy research. ML techniques have already proven successful in elucidating the relationships between structural and chemical features of HEAs and their resulting properties. This review comprehensively examines current efforts to leverage ML for analyzing alloy systems, with particular emphasis on property modeling, phase diagram determination, and reverse engineering. It also highlights various data-driven strategies, including Bayesian optimization, and outlines future prospects within the field.

Opportunities to utilize probabilistic modeling methods are growing due to the availability of vast datasets. Nevertheless, many practical challenges lack the data volume required to estimate parameters through traditional maximum likelihood techniques. While data-efficient models, often employing Few Shot Learning (FSL), aim to address this issue by using prior knowledge and transferring insights from other tasks, these approaches can introduce significant bias when the problem domain shifts between training and testing. Consequently, there is a need for methods that integrate prior information without such bias, allowing for robust learning from minimal samples. This study explores a hybrid approach combining Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with Functional Differential Equations (FDEs) to achieve this goal. By representing prior knowledge as graphs and letting GNNs propagate node features along weighted edges, the resulting latent variables serve as inputs for parsing time-ordered series via fitted FPDEs. Evaluated on both real and synthetic datasets, this framework demonstrates an enhanced ability to differentiate problems based on few data points and to generalize effectively in noisy, non-stationary environments.

Extensive experimental results demonstrate the method's superior performance in both speed and accuracy, leading to practical real-world deployments in three distinct locational contexts.

Federated semi-supervised learning (FSSL) combines the privacy benefits of federated learning with the cost-effectiveness of semi-supervised learning, utilizing scattered data across multiple clients that contains abundant unlabeled information alongside a small core set of labeled data. Nevertheless, current FSSL approaches face two major obstacles: (1) they fail to effectively leverage unlabeled data due to client-specific data distribution discrepancies, and (2) they suffer from inefficient label propagation across domains, resulting in cross-client ambiguity during the training process. To address these issues, we introduce AmbReg, a novel framework that simultaneously performs domain alignment to mitigate domain shift and uncertainty regularization to optimize the use of unlabeled data. Domain alignment ensures consistent statistical distributions across all clients, allowing model weights trained on labeled data to be aggregated uniformly without domain bias. Concurrently, the optimization of model outputs is guided by minimizing variance in the predicted label distribution, with this loss integrated directly into the federated learning objective. This guidance reduces the ambiguity surrounding label inference, thereby enhancing the reliability of using unlabeled data. Extensive testing across various datasets and experimental results indicate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

Magnetically influenced processes in compact-object binary mergers significantly impact general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics and emission across the electromagnetic spectrum. This study utilizes high-fidelity, general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations incorporating neutrino radiation to examine how variations in initial magnetic field intensity, magnetic geometry, and equations of state affect outcomes following black hole-neutron star encounters. We conduct 12 detailed simulations, each using a magnetic field of $\sim 10^{14}$ G with a configuration aligned to the neutron star's angular momentum, but differing in energy equation formulations and physical parameters. Our results indicate that while final electromagnetic emissions remain relatively consistent, magnetic field impacts on the immediate post-merger quench are minor, likely due to strong neutrino heating disrupting field advection and alignment with flow before the system coalescence. Additionally, we observe a negligible amount of post-merger electromagnetic jet activity, as the accretion disk forms a large, fat torus that prevents efficient magnetic flux amplification and collimation.

We present a distorted version of the Dirac operator on a closed, oriented Riemann surface equipped with a metric of constant negative curvature. By applying the Residue Theorem from complex analysis, we derive formulas determining both the index and the local index of this operator. These formulas particularly reveal how the local index correlates with the geometry and topology of the surface. Additionally, we establish conditions ensuring that this operator possesses a discrete spectrum.

This study introduces the new concept of consistent convergence to a Q-process. It establishes both a theorem characterizing this convergence and its application to the study of homogeneous Markov processes. The results demonstrate that consistent convergence to a single Q-process is equivalent to characteristic core equivalence between two core kernels. Furthermore, it proves a representation theorem for cores by showing that every Q-process corresponds to an assortment of cores, where each corresponds to an irreducible, conservative, and conservative-type Markov chain. Finally, the paper presents the application of these findings to a specific class of homogeneous Markov processes, specifically those on a countable state space where the underlying transition matrix possesses a Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue of one. By applying these theorems, it proves a convergence theorem for such processes, extending many of the theorems originally developed by R. A. Green for similar scenarios.

This work presents a theoretical investigation into the optical adherence of a bilayer system composed of nonlocal dielectric materials separated by a graphene monolayer. Utilizing a quantum mechanical framework for dielectric responses and solving the Schrödinger equation for electrons within the graphene layer, the study analyzes surface plasmons under both electrostatic and dynamic conditions. By examining the optical pressure, the research explores how thick-ene r values and monolayer parameters influence the adhesive forces between nanoscale colloid nanoparticles. Findings reveal that nonlocal effects substantially boost adherence, with graphene's unique ability to sustain Terahertz plasmons further amplifying optical adherence to exceptional levels. These results offer critical insights for photonic technologies involving surface plasmons and simultaneously clarify the structural assembly forces in carbon-based architectures, including fullerenes, carbon nanotubes, and related materials.

Interventions within a healthcare context, such as advertising for new services or implementing smoking cessation programs in the Emergency Department (ED), often aim to induce increased future ED visits. Researchers frequently employ difference-in-differences (DiD) analyses using Poisson or negative binomial direct modeling to assess the impact of such interventions on ED attendance. However, existing literature, including healthcare-specific examples, has not yet determined the prevalence of such pre-existing trends prior to implementation in an implementation. This absence is problematic because the validity of using pre-intervention data for model specification and validation relies on these data reflecting the same post-intervention processes. In this work, we address this gap by investigating the "typical" temporal response patterns observed in ED settings. Using a comprehensive dataset of 30 million visits and 30 simulated scenarios, we find that response curves are non-stationary in the short term but often exhibit long-term stationary behavior over weeks or months. Specifically, certain interventions demonstrate immediate decreases in ED visits followed by sustained increases in subsequent months. These trends have critical methodological implications: utilizing pre-intervention data for short-term di/long-term di/analysis risks introducing specification misspecification, a problem that can be mitigated through flexible non-parametric estimation techniques.

This paper addresses tactical cooperation for autonomous agents within robot networks with constrained computational, energy, and networking resources. We present a framework and associated algorithms for agents and networks constrained by limited bandwidth, packet loss, and latency. These capabilities are implemented using established communication protocols and hardware, ensuring their viability for application in current robotic systems. A primary contribution of this work is a protocol that enables agents to construct tactics based on compressed, efficient, and real-time interaction messages, reducing both the amount of data transmitted and the processing overhead for agent-based decision-making. Tackets are formed by organizing individual actions into structured trees, where leaves represent action messages and internal nodes consist of nodes. These internal nodes execute conditionally branching logic, process incoming signals, and determine the path the tree follows. We also define a method for compactly encoding the decision-trees, which minimizes memory usage and transmission volumes without sacrificing the capacity to store comprehensive decision strategies. The validity and applicability of this approach were tested in a TTP-based environment, demonstrating both network and agent constraint relief when compared to alternative techniques.

This study examines how the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) might influence charge-ordered correlations relative to the reaction plane in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions, using data from the ALICE experiment at the LHC with center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{\it{s}_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ = 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. While no significant CME-related signal was detected compared to S+S collisions, the investigation explores the effect's potential impact within a phenomenological three-plane geometry. Findings from this framework suggest that the influence of the CME on charge-ordered correlations relative to the reaction plane remains subtle even under the most favorable conditions: the effect is confined to the 1–2% level at $\sqrt{\it{s}_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ = 5.02 TeV and remains negligible or absent at $\sqrt{\it{s}_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ = 2.76 TeV.

The rapid growth of online fundraising platforms has enabled the emergence of various crowd-sourcing initiatives, ranging from offering rewards to simply seeking personal support in times of crisis. The primary focus of these platforms often centers on the fundraising process and the online community's reaction to a project. While existing literature primarily stems from computer science and operations research, the fields of social sciences and economics have contributed relatively little to understanding crowd dynamics within this context. Consequently, online communities and their associated crowd events remain largely unexplained in terms of social mechanisms, prompting current research to address this gap.

This study investigates online crowds using an original set of specific indicators. Employing rigorous methodology, the research compares four major fundraising platforms—two within the commercial sector and two within the volunteer sector—acquired through data scraping. It then analyzes the resulting information through a scientific lens by examining the derived indicators and their correlations. Ultimately, the conclusions and recommendations derived from this analysis are intended to provide valuable insights for the online fundraising industry, with broader potential applications across the research of online communities and crowd phenomena as well.

Data privacy concerns and the high costs associated with operational modifications often prevent individual organizations from deploying advanced intelligence-sharing systems (ISSs) dedicated to disseminating cyber hazard data. Moreover, the rapid evolution of hacking techniques continuously expands the cyber threat landscape, necessitating that ISSs be established rapidly and remain constantly updated. To address these challenges, this paper introduces the Privacy-Preserving Cyber Hazard ISS (PPCHISS), a novel system designed to mitigate those specific barriers. Underpinned by a federated learning architecture, PPCHISS enables participating organizations to jointly train a global intrusion detection model training data locally without transmitting sensitive raw data, thereby safeguarding local privacy. Evaluations against both real and synthetic datasets confirm the system's efficacy in protecting organizational data privacy. Furthermore, PPCHISS was compared with the centralized learning and differential privacy (DP) strategies. Results demonstrate that PPCHISS achieves the highest accuracy in anomaly detection and incurs the lowest communication and storage transmission costs. Additionally, the system was rigorously tested regarding robustness to malicious nodes and practical deployment difficulties.

Robotic manipulation is a fundamental and widely researched domain within robotics, yet extending this to simultaneous multi-point handling remains a significant challenge. The core issue involves determining an optimal sequencing of robotic tasks to maximize efficiency. To tackle this complexity, this paper introduces a new Greedy Clustering-Oriented ManiPulation (GCOM) strategy. Unlike many existing approaches for complex sequencing problems, GCOM does not rely on computation heavy optimizations such as Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP). Instead, it begins by partitioning all tasks into subgroups based on their goal locations and then employs an L1-norm regularized Support Vector Regressor (LSVR) to calculate travel times between robots for these clusters. Utilizing these estimated transitions, the method adopts a greedy algorithm to determine the final execution order for both the clusters and individual tasks within them. Evaluated against various scenarios across three experimental metrics—completion time, energy usage, and carbon emissions—the L1-norm based SVM regression models used in GPCM are assessed and compared against two state-of-the-art non-optimal sequencing methods. Results indicate a superior performance by GCOM, delivering shorter task durations and reduced electricity consumption. Additionally, the proposed framework is flexible enough to incorporate external constraints, such as robot carbon footprints, when planning sequences.

This paper explores how cognitive alignment within teams influences performance. We begin by introducing the standard of synchronisation: teams must synchronize not only externally with market demands but also internally among team members. Focusing on make teams that satisfy both conditions, we analyze three key questions. First, does a team's parameter heterogeneity affect its level of synchronisation and, consequently, its performance? Second, in scenarios where a team is locked into a trapped equilibrium, can we achieve untrapped equilibrium through collaboration with another team, and what are the implications for per-capcapcap performance in these untrapped states? Third, does a team achieve higher per-capcapcap performance by establishing links with another team? Addressing these questions, we find that heterogeneity in team parameters leads to lower performance, and while a team with a make market and untrapped equilibrium achieves better results by connecting with another team, the findings suggest that collaboration with another team can also result in higher per-capcapcap performance when at least one team is heterogeneously composed, even if other conditions are met. However, connecting with another team does not guarantee improved performance for all members. On the issue of trapped equilibria, collaboration with another team helps a team escape trapping only if at least one team is heterogeneously composed; but connecting with another team may actually increase the likelihood of trapping for homogeneous teams. These insights provide valuable guidance for managers seeking to build effective make teams.

Users frequently employ video search engines to locate specific content, yet these platforms currently lack the in-depth user experience evaluation that text-centric search engines have received. Current practices for assessing video search rely on methods like click-through rates, A/B testing, and subjective surveys, but each is limited by an inability to simultaneously gauge multiple variables or detect subtle biases. To address this, this paper introduces VAE/Virtual Agent Experience, the first automated system dedicated to video-specific search auditing. This tool simulates diverse real-world user personas and their contextual needs, a capability crucial for validating user variety, while also using agent reactions to identify origin variety bias. These findings imply that operators $T$ related by a monotropic coupling can only differ in a discrete set of quantum numbers, specifically a discrete set. Current medium access control (MAC) protocols are constrained by backlogs that cause interference correlations, degrading performance in wireless communication. We propose a novel stochastic MAC framework where nodes transmit randomly, without adhering to specific protocols, by pulling transmission opportunities from a shared pool. Targeting medium-density, interference-correlated environments, our model integrates both statistical properties and physical layer constraints into an analytical evaluation of throughput and delay. Guided by this analysis, we introduce a non-adaptive retransmission strategy that optimally balances throughput and latency. Simulations comparing our approach against standard MAC benchmarks demonstrate significant performance gains, and numerical results further validate our analytical models.

Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective for node classification, they typically demand extensive labeled datasets. To address this, semi-supervised frameworks using pseudo-labeling have emerged, relying on initial labels to train a classifier that generates pseudo-labels for all nodes. However, these existing methods often fail in an low-label setting because initial training gets overfitted to the scarce labeled nodes, causing the pseudo-labels for unlabelled nodes to be inaccurate. To overcome this, we introduce a novel approach called SL2S—Shortcut Loss with Separation—that mitigates label collapse. Our method employs a multi-class separate shortcut to integrate separate losses with a multi-task learning strategy, ensuring the classifier remains robust even when trained on very few labeled nodes. Additionally, a separate pseudo-label filtering step is used to eliminate inaccurate labels prior to knowledge distillation between strong and weak models to boost performance. Extensive tests in the SL2S across various synthetic and real-world graphs confirm that it surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces PatchNet, a novel architecture designed for processing video content. PatchNet aligns short-range templates by performing convolutional feature matching between image patches and corresponding kernel patches. This mechanism enables the neural network to utilize computational methods established by traditional handcrafted optical flow techniques, specifically achieving full-frame feature extraction with constant computational complexity. Experiments conducted on multiple video tasks, including fluid prediction and motion estimation, demonstrate performance that rivals state-of-the-art models with significantly lower memory requirements. Additionally, the approach facilitates efficient hardware deployment through sparse operations and fully convolutional structures. When executed on consumer-grade hardware, inference occurs at a steady rate of 200 fps.

This study examines optimal resource allocation—specifically transmission power, spectral efficiency, bandwidth, transmission rate, frame duration, and sampling frequency—for a millimeter-wave integrated system offering diverse multi-services, including millimeter-wave communications and energy harvesting for IoT applications, within a finite set of finite states. The primary objective is to maximize the weighted sum of utility functions, tailored to specific communication and energy needs, subject to channel, hardware, and service-level constraints. The resulting non-convex optimization challenge is transformed into an equivalent convex formulation by decomposing bandwidth and power allocation tasks. Consequently, a closed-form solution is derived for power allocation, while bandwidth allocation follows an explicit analytical approach based on system requirements. Communications parameters are determined through a specialized analytical method. Utility weights are calculated using a TILe (Tailored to Information Leakage) framework within a Markov Decision Process to enhance long-term performance. Finally, simulation analyses validate the proposed architecture and resource management strategies, demonstrating a higher utility achievement in multi-service environments compared to single-service baselines.

This work demonstrates that classical electromechanics—a field exploring the interaction between mechanical motion and electromagnetic fields—can be accurately represented by hybrid electrical circuits. We establish a duality between these systems and conventional optomechanics, a regime involving both classical and optical components. By leveraging this theoretical parallel, we outline a framework for realizing key principles of microwave optomechanics utilizing microwave electronics. Specifically, we reveal a feasibility route to achieve strong coupling through on-chip transformer impedance transformation. Furthermore, we propose a feedback scheme utilizing circuit-based electronics to explore optomechanics with external delay loops. This configuration enables the investigation of superstable limit limit-cycle oscillators and spectral density spectral enhancement through mechanical backaction.

Polynomials exhibiting Airy-like behavior emerge during the random polygon non-intersecting constraint (IPR) transformation when a specific limit is applied. They serve as generalizations of Airy polynomials, defined recursively through an "Airy scheme of equations." It has been demonstrated that these polynomials possess entire function status, comply with diverse combinatorial identities, and exhibit orthogonality with respect to a specific weight function defined on a bounded interval. Furthermore, a particular subclass corresponds precisely to transfer-matrix eigenfunctions associated with uniform self-avoiding walks originating from the critical point. In the large-degree asymptotic regime, these polynomials approach Airy functions, with their zeros converging to those of the Airy function itself.

Lapararoscopic surgery stands as one of the most extensively utilized minimally invasive surgical techniques, renowned for delivering superior visual clarity. Despite these advantages, certain conditions inherently reduce visibility within specific surgical sites. Tobacco smoke serves as a significant example within endoscopic gastroenterology, a context where detecting tobacco use is critical. Nevertheless, identifying smoke images poses considerable challenges due to their scarcity within surgical footage. This paper introduces an innovative approach to locating smoke within such contexts, leveraging image enhancement as a complementary strategy. Enhancement was implemented to amplify characteristics associated with smoke, such as movement and blur. Consequently, it was determined that enhancing laparoscopic imagery can indeed benefit the process of identifying smoke images, with a proposed method achieving 81.6% recall, 70.7% precision, a false-positive rate of 14.3%, and demonstrating a false-negative rate of 18.4%.

The Mølmer–Sørensen approach is a widely recognized technique in trapped-ion architectures, utilizing coupled optical and electronic interactions alongside shared ionic motion to implement entangling operations. For durations spanning several motional cycles, such as long-range gates, achieving the required amplitude consistency and phase alignment across different modes proves challenging, necessitating high-precision control. However, we demonstrate that a specific superposition of these various modes mitigates sensitivity to individual mode parameters, effectively enhancing gate fidelity. Notably, we present a simple radio frequency configuration enabling a $\pi$-rotation along the $x$-axis that utilizes equal contributions from all modes, thereby realizing high-fidelity MS interactions even when individual modes are excited only over a limited range, or poorly.

Perforated micrographs featuring the complex-logic arrangement of paraelectric perovskites are engineered by applying Gaussian smoothing to atomic-scale data. This macroscopic depiction effectively identifies the boundaries between unit cells, which are arranged in hexagonal and cubic perforations, similar to those seen in optical lenses, and is highly consistent with experimental Scanning Probe Microscopy (SPM) findings. This quantitative study demonstrates that the phonon-induced atomic vibrations and thermal fluctuations are essential factors explaining why real-world results often differ from predictions made by ideal spin-lattice models. Consequently, a novel statistical model grounded in lattice-structure phonons is introduced, which can account for experimental observations across the widest range of perovskite parameters, spanning from small to large lattices and various spin configurations. This methodology offers significant utility in characterizing experimental data, analyzing performance, guiding future investigations, and designing new materials.

The proposed approach's efficacy is validated through simulations, as well *as* a real-world analysis of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data.

Average-case analysis of sorting within convex quadratic equivalence classes of comparison programs reveals that within each class, nearly all algorithms perform nearly identically across diverse input distributions. This phenomenon, known as "local universality," indicates that for any specific distribution $D$, average-case behavior is dictated solely by the support of $D$; furthermore, as $D$ approaches its statistical limit—defined by the support alone—its behavior becomes increasingly consistent and predictable. A key outcome of these findings is a novel method for defining and quantifying sorting lower bounds: any class exhibiting local average-case universality must reach a minimum level of total cost equal to the class-optimal average-case cost for sorting from randomness. In this framework, we provide the first comprehensive analysis of convex quadratic programs while delivering near-tight bounds for nearly all such classes. Notably, we identify several previously unrecognized sorting lower-bound classes and propose a strictly inferior class of seemingly viable algorithms that still defy intuitive design principles for efficiency, suggesting that the average worst-case performance in this case drops even further than previously conjectured.

Global Positioning Systems (GPS) are widely used for navigation and locating objects, but their susceptibility to interference and disruption poses significant risks for mission success. As a viable alternative, using Time of Arrival (ToA) measurements from Communication Transfer Functions (CTFs) allows for localization and tracking in GPS-denied environments. Given that GPs is also vulnerable within indoor settings for this CTF-based approach, there is an urgent need for a robust PDA algorithm capable of filtering out faulty nodes to ensure reliable tracking. Motivated by this, we present a novel Resilient Adaptive PD A method that combines CTFs with an Adaptive Rejection strategy to accurately locate and follow targets under challenging conditions. The core of this process is a multi-stage detection procedure: first, we filter CTFs with very weak amplitudes to reduce computational load; second, for a set of remaining strong CTFs, our algorithm identifies anomalous measurements that could skew position estimates. The effectiveness of this Resilient method, which outperforms existing techniques, has been verified through simulations and a practical indoor experiment.

This study details the observation and measurement of $W^{\pm}Z$ boson production in proton-proton interactions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV using the ATLAS detector at the LHC, based on a dataset corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $36~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$. The analysis focuses on decaying hadronic and leptonic channels of the Z boson, specifically investigating properties such as transverse momentum, charge asymmetry, and $\ell^\pm\ell'^{\mp}W^{\pm}$ scattering angles for final-state leptons. These results are compared against Standard Model predictions from MADGRAPH5_AMC@NLO and POWHEG, as well as further models employing PYTHIA8 parton showers, with good overall agreement found. Additionally, production rates are evaluated using next-to-leading order (NLO) QCD predictions from POWHEG combined with PYTHIA8, showing consistency as well. Joint-polarization fractions of the Z boson in different final-state topologies were also derived and matched well with standard model simulations using SOFA. Finally, parameters of the effective field theory, including constraints on the dimensionless coefficient $C_{\varphi D}$ from the dimension-6 operator $\mathcal{O}_{\varphi D}$, were investigated within the Standard Model Effective Field Framework framework.

In the context of large-scale Interior Point Methods (IPMs), efficiently solving linear systems is crucial, with the widely adopted Minimal Residual (MINRES) method within AutotT requiring significantly fewer iterations than prior art. This paper introduces a novel termination criterion based on a user-defined tolerance applied to both relative and absolute residual norms. By doing so, it allows users to reduce total IPM execution time further by prematurely ending MINRES iterations when their contribution to overall efficiency diminish. An empirical analysis confirms that applying this new criterion can save more computation time than simply following standard recommended IPM parameters.

Practical AI systems destined for public deployment face the risk of malfunctioning due to practical constraints, thereby causing harm to users or other detrimental outcomes. Since many of these error categories are predictable and reversible through adequate pre-mitigation, ensuring public AI systems operate safely demands the adoption of proactive methodologies. By cataloging past failures, organizations can implement targeted measures averting the very issues documented in the repository, thereby enhancing the overall safety of deployed systems.

We establish the universal lower bound on entropy production when transforming an equilibrium system into another equilibrium system through arbitrary rapid processes, demonstrating that this production cannot fall below the value derived from the free-energy landscape of the start and end states. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a pivotal driver in global ecological advancements, enabling condition monitoring, pollution tracking, and sustainability analysis. Yet, these AI applications carry inherent environmental footprints, primarily stemming from electricity usage during model training and deployment. Consequently, an AI solution intended to address environmental issues often generates concealed ecological costs that must be contrasted with the benefits it offers. This study introduces a comprehensive framework assessing the net environmental impact of AI models by integrating carbon metrics with dual benefit-contribution dimensions: direct contributions, such as efficient condition monitoring, and indirect contributions, such as facilitating informed policy. The proposed net impact formula integrates AI development time, inference phases, and carbon data with these benefit types to yield a net carbon outcome. Validated through an experimental deployment of two distinct carbon-based machine learning models—designed respectively for identifying pollution hotspots and forecasting carbon emissions—the findings demonstrate a consistent alignment between the models' predicted long-term carbon offsets and the actual environmental advantages realized.

Prescriptive procedure monitoring (PresMo) focuses on analyzing process event data to pinpoint processes in need of improvements. While PresMo has seen rapid development recently, many existing solutions remain underutilized in practice. This paper explores the current state of PresMo by defining key dimensions—specifically the methods for calculating performance and improvement strategies, along with their support levels—and examines how PresMo adoption has evolved over the last decade through a systematic review of literature from 2011 to 2021. Findings indicate a growing interest in PresMo research, yet improvements are still needed in the adoption of data-driven approaches and the integration of machine learning. Based on these insights, several avenues for future investigation are proposed, including: (1) investigating ways to dynamically adjust prescription recommendations; (2) further developing data-driven prescription techniques and employing machine learning for enhanced process recommendations; and (3) more closely aligning PresMo models with the realities of professional environments.

This approach calculates and utilizes local approximation errors for both the temperature field and specific quantities of interest, most of which are defined post-computation through a preliminary multilocal simulation run. This initial run is followed by the main adaptive loop, during which a single simulation produces multiple outputs, including the definition of error metrics required for the process.

This method represents a computationally efficient adaptation that achieves accurate multigoal-focused control by reducing the necessity for multiple sequential simulations. Additionally, we address the issue of adapting the computational grid based on results, and in this context, we present an analysis that guarantees optimal local error estimates. This analysis applies to a broad category of problems, allowing for flexible modeling. Kernelization serves as a method to address the central challenge of narrative interface mining: the excessive volume of extracted user stories necessitates their compression into an equivalent form of shorter length. Existing approaches fall into two categories. The first involves heuristics such as text compression algorithms and statistics-driven item removal, which suffer from format-format specificity and text format dependency alongside poor quality. The second approach utilizes item kernels—structures that compute the shared textual element between two items to achieve compression. However, this method results in kernels that are difficult to read, fail to preserve the original structure, and remain inconsistent in their representation.

This paper introduces **Stacking Kernel**, the inaugural kernelization technique specifically tailored to maintain the hierarchical structure inherent in user stories. It achieves this by employing **diff-based text stacking** combined with **synonym-based text stacking**. To evaluate its efficacy, we established **Staple**, an extensive dataset of user stories and a corresponding evaluation framework. Furthermore, a **baseline model** constructed using only synonym-based stacking was developed to facilitate this study. Experimental results indicate that the full Stacking Kernel outperforms the baseline by delivering superior synonym count reduction and shorter resulting texts. Moreover, both models demonstrate significant improvement over current baseline methods. Beyond performance, we conducted a human-centric study to assess usability, readability, and overall satisfaction. This analysis confirms that the full Stacking Kernel surpasses the baseline model and aligns closely with the preferences of human practitioners.

Although cells convert genetic information into proteins to sustain life, the precise mechanisms underlying the synthesis of messenger RNA (mRNA) remain incompletely understood. Existing models focusing on the nuclear accumulation of mRNA typically assume that rates of transcription and nuclear export are directly proportional, ignoring potential complexities. In contrast, our study utilizes a comprehensive mathematical framework to analyze dynamic data from both mRNA and protein levels, revealing distinct patterns in transcription dynamics. We observe two primary scenarios: first, when translation efficiency varies, transcription rates may vary independently of translation; second, under conditions where translation remains constant, transcription rates remain uniform regardless of the number of transcripts produced. Crucially, we detected a consistent lag between transcription initiation and nuclear accumulation of mRNA, which correlates with lower overall mRNA stability. These findings suggest that transcription is a multi-step process mediated by distinct molecular complexes, where initiation and subsequent steps are tightly coupled by mechanisms including coupling and genetic buffering, resulting in observable temporal delays in transcriptional response.

This study investigates the physical nature of the unexpectedly observed, unusually long-lived (J^*=0+) state in 64Ni, a gamma-ray doublet at 44 keV arising from its decay. Using the interacting boson-fermion model, we successfully demonstrate that this state emerges from the coupling of a fermion to an 0_4^+ boson. Our findings indicate that this specific coupling is facilitated by the Monopole Tensor (MT) force, thereby providing strong evidence that the 0_4^+ state in 64Ni forms through the interaction of particles with collective bosons. We anticipate that the systematic analysis of 0_4^+ states across various nuclei will further validate the physical significance of the Monopole Tensor interaction.

Recent attempts within non-supersymmetric gauge theories with $N$ loops of dualities have struggled due to the vast number of distinct configurations, particularly for theories featuring simple gauge groups. This study identifies and analyzes various classes of chiral gauge theories, including $SU(N)$ models with only abelian fermions, $SU(N)$ theories with chiral non-$U(1)$ fermions, and theories based on exceptional groups. For the $SU(N)$ with abional fermions case, known duality configurations are examined, while the authors propose extensions of these dualities as well as entirely dual, non-mirror pairs. These constructions rely heavily on analyzing global symmetries; specifically, any anomalous global symmetry serves as an unambiguous marker to distinguish theories in terms of their infrared dynamics. The paper concludes by examining the anomaly structures associated with these global symmetries in $SU(N)$ with abional fermions, exceptional group theories, and $SU(N)$ theories with non-$U(1)$ chiral fermions, assessing each to determine how many theories are sufficiently simple that their duality relationships can be fully established through their global symmetries alone.

Exact optimization and inference within discrete graphical models are notoriously difficult, especially as problem scales grow, largely because of the numerous local extrema that complicate finding the global optimum. Although inference in probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) addresses constrained optimization, this constraint structure is often overlooked, potentially hindering the use of tailored algorithms designed to leverage such properties. This paper introduces a novel graphical model constructed from constraint graphs to represent the feasible solution space, thereby enabling PGMs with discrete constraints to benefit from inference techniques intended for structured constrained optimization. Our primary objective is to enable faster convergence to exact solutions—whether via constraint relaxation or alternative methods—by exploiting the resulting constraint graph's typically sparser structure compared to the original model. We validate our methodology on discrete convex optimization tasks, including the unimodal-at-a-time (UAMP) reconstruction of rank-one matrices and discrete convex polytomous logistic regression, demonstrating that our approach yields more rapid convergence to exact results than prior art.
